intro.html: Explained like you're 12. Ordered so each word only uses words defined above it.
How an entry is written. One definition line and two optional italic lines under it:

• **term** — what it means. The definition, written for someone who has read only the entries above this one.
  • *Example: one concrete value.* A real value from the work, never an invented one.
  • *Context: where it is used · source: path/to/owner.md · related: [term](#slug), [other](#slug) · see: [label](#anchor) · first seen 2026-09-05* The metadata. Segments are separated by · (or ; before a key); every segment is optional. source: names the one repo-relative file that owns the term, related: the entries this one leans on, see: a figure, exhibit or page worth opening. first seen is normally left out — app/tools/gen-dictionary.mjs derives it from git, taking the author date of the earliest commit that added the term's bold marker to this file, and you only write it by hand for a term that existed in the work before it reached this page.
The Learn page renders those as the definition, the example beneath it, and a quiet metadata footer carrying the date, the source, the related entries as links, and the exhibits.

Concrete values in *Example:* lines are illustrations, not the source of truth for a measurement. Dataset numbers are owned by ../ideation/data-findings.md; repository and infrastructure numbers by current-state.md.

Diagrams: mermaid blocks render automatically on GitHub, in VS Code with the Markdown preview, and on Obsidian/Notion. If you are reading this in a plain text editor they will look like code — open it on GitHub instead. Colour code used everywhere: green = good / safe / the goal, red = broken / dangerous / lost points, yellow = a decision point, blue = neutral machinery, purple = the raw input. Every diagram is followed by a > **Legend** line decoding its own colours and symbols, so you never have to guess what a shape means.

chapters.title: DNA basics (read this first, everything else needs it)

blocks.html: the instruction book inside every cell. Written with only 4 letters: A, C, G, T.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ...ACGGTTACG... A human book is 3 billion letters long.

blocks.html: one letter of DNA (A, C, G, or T).
DNA is two strands zipped together; A always pairs with T, C with G. One rung of the ladder = 1 bp.
blocks.exampleHtml: 1 kb = 1,000 letters. 1 Mb = 1 million letters. 1 Gbp = 1 billion letters.

blocks.alt: DNA ladder: A pairs with T, C pairs with G
blocks.legendHtml: each coloured box is one DNA letter · A always faces T, C always faces G · the bracket on the left marks one base pair.

blocks.html: the whole instruction book of one person (all 3 billion letters).
the book is split into 23 volumes. Written chr1, chr2, ... chr15, chrX, chrY.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: chr15q15.1 = chromosome 15, long arm (q), region 15.1. Like "volume 15, page 15, paragraph 1".

blocks.alt: How to read the address chr15q15.1
blocks.legendHtml: blue: the chromosome body · gray oval: the centromere, the pinch in the middle · red stripe: the band being addressed · yellow boxes: the four parts of the address, in order.

blocks.html: one recipe inside the book. About 20,000 recipes. Each makes one protein.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the gene BUB1B is the recipe for a protein that checks cell division.

blocks.html: the machine the recipe builds. Proteins do all the actual work in a cell.
one bead in the protein chain. A gene's letters, read 3 at a time, spell out which bead comes next.

blocks.alt: DNA letters grouped in threes become amino acids
blocks.legendHtml: gray boxes: DNA letters · the brackets show how they group in threes · each circle is the amino acid that triple codes for · red circle: STOP, the end of the recipe.

blocks.html: the parts of a gene that end up in the final recipe (the useful text).
the parts cut out and thrown away before the recipe is used (like commercials cut from a recorded show).

the part of the exons that is actually translated into protein. Exons also carry untranslated ends (UTRs); the CDS is the recipe proper. About 1 % of the genome, plus the stop codon that ends it. Nearly every variant that breaks a protein sits in the CDS or within a few bases of its edges.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ressources/reference/coding_regions.tsv — every CDS of every protein-coding transcript, widened by 8 bases on each side and merged per gene: 223,048 intervals, 44.6 Mb (methodology 069).

blocks.html: the few intronic bases on each side of an exon that the splicing machinery reads. A change there can wreck splicing without touching the CDS itself. The ±2 bases are the canonical splice sites (almost always damaging); VEP's splice_region_variant reaches ±8. That is why the coding intervals above are widened by 8, not 0.
the cutting-out step. Cell removes introns, glues exons together.
blocks.exampleHtml: If splicing goes wrong, the recipe is garbled and the protein is broken.

blocks.legendHtml: green boxes: exons, kept · gray boxes: introns, cut out and thrown away · yellow hexagon: the splicing step · blue: the finished recipe · purple: the protein it builds.

blocks.html: a change buried far inside an intron, far from any exon. Easy to miss, but can still wreck splicing.
one specific version of a recipe (a gene can be spliced several ways). MANE Select = the one official version everyone agrees to quote.

the one version Ensembl nominates as the gene's representative, and the one every tool reports against by default. It matters that everybody uses the same one: an exon number, a domain boundary and a variant's amino-acid position are only comparable if they are all measured on the same transcript. Example: ENST00000287598 for BUB1B; Ensembl writes the pointer with a version suffix (.11) that the transcript's own id lacks.

Ensembl's label for what kind of thing a gene or transcript is. It is a classification, not a measurement, and the one that matters most is whether the thing makes a protein. Software analogy: a type tag on a record — you branch on it before deciding which fields are even meaningful. Example: protein_coding for BUB1B, lncRNA for DICER1-AS1, protein_coding_CDS_not_defined for a BUB1B transcript that is annotated but has no reading frame.

a gene that is copied into RNA and then stops there: the RNA is the product, and no protein is ever built from it. "Long" just means over ~200 bases; "non-coding" is the load-bearing half. It still has real exons and is still spliced, so an exon track for one is honest — but it has no amino acids, no protein domains and no fold, so every protein-level question about it is not "unknown", it is "not applicable". Many lncRNAs sit head-to-head with a protein-coding gene and are named after it with an -AS1 suffix, meaning antisense — read from the opposite strand at the same locus. Example: DICER1-AS1 (ENSG00000235706) overlaps DICER1's far end on chr14 and makes no protein; asking this project's /api/panel/protein-structure for it answers 422, not an empty fold.

the short human name of a gene, assigned by HGNC (the committee that owns human gene naming). It is the label everyone actually says out loud, and it is not a stable identifier: HGNC renames genes, and the old name becomes a previous symbol. A gene also collects aliases — informal names from papers and older nomenclature — which are not authoritative either. Software analogy: the symbol is a mutable display name, the Ensembl ENSG… id is the primary key; join on the key, show the name. Example: CENATAC was renamed from CCDC84 in 2020 (HGNC:30460), and p31comet is an alias for MAD2L1BP that no database is obliged to resolve.

the REST call that turns a gene symbol into a stable id: GET rest.ensembl.org/lookup/symbol/homo_sapiens/<symbol>?expand=1, which answers with the gene record and, with expand=1, every transcript. Two traps, both verified live in this project: it resolves the current symbol only — CCDC84 gets a flat 400 {"error":"No valid lookup found for symbol CCDC84"} — and the sibling endpoint GET /xrefs/symbol/homo_sapiens/<symbol>, which searches cross-references instead, does resolve a retired symbol but answers with a list of matches. So an alias is confirmed by the target id appearing in that list, never by the list having one entry: CCDC84 returns two ids, both of which are CENATAC (one on the primary assembly, one on a patch scaffold). Example: /lookup/symbol/homo_sapiens/BUB1B?expand=1 → ENSG00000156970, biotype: protein_coding, canonical_transcript: ENST00000287598.11.

which of the DNA's two mirrored strands a gene is read from. Forward / plus (+1) reads left-to-right along the coordinate axis, reverse / minus (-1) reads right-to-left. Consequence: on a minus-strand gene, exon 1 is the rightmost box on a chart. Example: TP53 is -1, BUB1B is +1.
the first base actually copied into the transcript, i.e. where reading begins. On the minus strand it is the gene's high coordinate.
one copy of a gene. You have 2 copies of every gene: one from each parent.

chapters.title: Reading DNA (sequencing) and the files it makes

blocks.html: machine reads the DNA letters. It cannot read the whole book at once, so it shreds it and reads tiny scraps.
one scrap the machine read. Typically 150 letters long.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this case is 2 × 149 letters.

blocks.html: a per-letter confidence number. Q30 means "1 chance in 1,000 this letter is wrong". People quote the Q30 rate: the share of letters at Q30 or better.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 92% Q30 in this dataset — good. Below ~80% and you start distrusting calls.

blocks.html: machine reads both ends of each scrap. Two files, R1 and R2, that pair up.

blocks.alt: Paired-end reads and the known gap between them
blocks.legendHtml: blue: the R1 read · orange: the R2 read · gray: the middle, never read · the arrows show which direction each end is read from.

blocks.html: the full length of the original scrap, R1 + the unread middle + R2. It is the physical reach of one piece of evidence.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 266 letters here. Two variants further apart than that can never sit on the same fragment, which is exactly why phasing fails at gene scale in this case.

blocks.html: the machine's own subdivisions. One library of DNA is spread across several lanes and read in parallel; the lane number is in every read's name.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: @A01973:164:HGWCNDSX7:1:… = instrument A01973 (a NovaSeq 6000), flowcell HGWCNDSX7, lane 1. This case is 4 lanes × 2 ends = 8 FASTQ files, all one library — so the lanes are technical repeats and you just merge them.

blocks.html: how many scraps cover each letter, on average. 30× = each letter was read ~30 times.
blocks.exampleHtml: More coverage = more confident. At 5× coverage, "nothing found here" means nothing.

blocks.text:
reference    A   C   G   T   T   A   C   G   T   A   C
read 1       A   C   G   T   T   A
read 2           C   G   T   T   A   C   G

Real data: ~30 scraps stacked on every letter (30x).
A hole in the stack is why "we found nothing in that exon" can be a lie.
blocks.legendHtml: each read row is one 150-letter scrap · the depth row counts how many scraps cover that letter · the thin edges are where a call becomes a coin flip.

blocks.html: read the entire book, introns and all. ~85 GB of data.
read only the exons (~2% of the book). Cheaper, but blind to introns.
blocks.exampleHtml: This case is WGS, so hidden intron answers ARE possible.

blocks.alt: WGS reads everything, WES reads only the 2 percent of exons
blocks.legendHtml: green ticks: exons · gray bar: the whole genome · the dashed row is what WES sees, the blue row is what WGS sees.

blocks.html: the raw scrap file. Just the letters + a quality score per letter. Huge, unorganized.
puzzle step: figure out where each scrap belongs on the reference book.
the standard "official" human book everyone compares against. Version 38.
blocks.exampleHtml: Positions only mean something relative to a reference. chr15:40,000,000 in GRCh38 ≠ same spot in GRCh37.

blocks.html: one continuous named sequence in the reference. Chromosomes are contigs; so is every leftover fragment nobody could place.
the same chromosome is written chr15 in some references and plain 15 in others. Both are GRCh38; only the string differs. Programs that compare names literally will silently find nothing.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this case's VCF says 15, the submission format demands chr15. Convert in exactly one place in your code, never by hand.

blocks.html: the standard way to write a stretch of the genome: a contig name, a colon, and a 1-based coordinate range that is inclusive at both ends. Every genome tool takes one (samtools view, bcftools view -r, IGV's search box), so it is the closest thing genomics has to a URL. Watch the off-by-one: interval files (the .bed format, further down) are 0-based and half-open, so the same stretch is written with a different start there.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 15:40100000-40200000 and chr15:40,100,000-40,200,000 name the same 100,001 bp window on chromosome 15; the commas are decoration and the chr is the prefix question above.

blocks.html: the packaging of a reference for real analysis. Alt contigs are alternative versions of tricky regions; a no-alt set leaves them out so each read has one obvious home. Decoy sequence (hs38d1) is junk DNA added deliberately as a magnet, so reads that belong nowhere stick to it instead of piling up on a real gene and inventing a variant.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this VCF declares 1,690 contigs — 25 real ones (1–22, X, Y, M), 148 unplaced fragments, and 1,517 decoys.

blocks.html: a real piece of human sequence that could not be pinned to a chromosome. Variants there are almost always noise for a diagnosis.
the file of scraps AFTER alignment (each scrap now has an address). CRAM = same thing, squeezed smaller.
a popular aligner program (does the puzzle step).
copies of the same original scrap, made during library prep, not real independent evidence. They get marked and ignored, so they cost you coverage.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 9.3% here — normal. That is part of why 52× of raw letters becomes ~44× of usable depth.

blocks.html: comparing the person's scraps to the reference and writing down every difference.
the program that does it. DeepVariant, GATK HaplotypeCaller, Clair3.
the list of differences. One line per difference. Much smaller than FASTQ.
blocks.exampleHtml: This is the main hunting ground.

blocks.legendHtml: purple: the real genome · red: raw and huge · yellow: aligned but still huge · green: small and usable · gray: the tools in between.

blocks.html: The whole hackathon is a fight over what got lost between red and green.
the caller's confidence flag on each line. PASS = caller trusts it. Non-PASS lines get thrown away by default — dangerous, because the real answer might be sitting there.
blocks.exampleHtml: It is a text column on a row the caller kept, not a deletion: GATK's VariantFiltration writes the name of every threshold the line failed and leaves the line in the file. So "suppressed" means downstream tools are expected to skip it. When a line trips several thresholds the names are packed into one ;-joined string, so LowQual;QD2 is one record that failed two tests — counting it once under each name over-counts the file. Software analogy: a warning level on a log line, not a dropped log line. Example: 271,414 of this callset's 5,012,204 lines are non-PASS — 5.4 %. What is inside those lines for the candidate genes is measured in methodology 049.

blocks.html: the aligner's confidence, in Phred units, that a read came from the place it put it. It is low wherever the genome repeats itself, because the same read could have come from two or more places and the aligner cannot tell which. Not the same thing as base quality, which is the instrument's confidence in each letter. Software analogy: confidence in which bucket a hash landed in, as opposed to confidence in the bytes.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: MAPQ 0 means "this read maps equally well somewhere else" — common in segmental duplications and near telomeres.

blocks.html: a FILTER label meaning the mean mapping quality at this site is under 40. It fires in hard-to-map sequence, so it is a statement about where the variant is, not about whether it is real — which is exactly why non-PASS lines are worth mining: a real variant sitting in a repeat gets flagged too.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the heaviest suppression reason in this callset — 177,522 lines, and 12 of the candidate panel's 20 suppressed lines.

blocks.html: the site's QUAL score divided by the read depth behind it. Raw QUAL grows with coverage, so a deeply covered site looks confident even on weak evidence; dividing normalises that out. Software analogy: a rate rather than a total.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the QD2 FILTER label = QD under 2, i.e. very little confidence per read. 35,402 lines here.

blocks.html: compression + a table-of-contents so you can jump to chr15 without reading the whole file.
checking the data isn't broken before trusting any result. Tools: FastQC, MultiQC, samtools stats, bcftools stats, mosdepth.
a sanity number: transitions divided by transversions (two chemically different kinds of letter swap). Real human WGS lands around 2.0–2.1. Way off = something is wrong.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 1.94 here — slightly noisy, acceptable.

blocks.html: the first column of every bcftools stats line, saying which table that line belongs to. One file holds a dozen stacked tables rather than one, so the code is how you tell them apart. Software analogy: a tagged-union log format — one line type per tag, and you dispatch on the tag. The ones this project reads: SN (summary numbers: records, SNPs, indels, multiallelic sites), TSTV (one row, the Ti/Tv ratio), ST (substitution spectrum: one row per A>C-style swap), IDD (indel length distribution, negative = deletion), DP (read depth distribution), AF (one row per non-reference allele-frequency bin — see the trap below), SiS (singleton stats: the counters for alleles seen exactly once).
blocks.exampleHtml: Two things about the delivered file are worth knowing. The AF section here is a zygosity split, not a frequency spectrum: it is computed from each record's own AC/AN, and with one sample AN is always 2, so bcftools emits exactly two bins — AC=1 (heterozygous) and AC=2 (homozygous alternate). Nothing about the general population is in it. And SiS is the same numbers again: bcftools prints the singleton counters once keyed by allele count and again as the first AF bin, so on this file the two lines are byte-identical. Which sections the delivery actually contains — and which it does not, QUAL included — is measured in methodology 045. Example: ST 0 A>G 656121 — section ST, sample id 0, 656,121 A-to-G substitutions.

blocks.html: modern Illumina instruments do not emit every possible Phred score. They round each one to a handful of representative values so the FASTQ compresses far better. So a "quality distribution" is genuinely a few tall bars, not a smooth curve — and plotting it as a density curve invents detail the instrument never recorded. Software analogy: lossy quantisation before compression, like reducing a colour palette.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this NovaSeq run uses exactly four levels — Phred 2, 11, 25 and 37 — measured in step-0/methodology/028.

blocks.html: a commercial re-implementation of the GATK variant-calling algorithms, much faster and giving near-identical results. Common in clinical labs, so you meet it in VCF headers rather than by choosing it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: this callset was made by Sentieon Haplotyper → Sentieon GVCFtyper → GATK VariantFiltration. Reading that chain tells you it is a small-variant pipeline only — no structural variants will ever appear in this file.

blocks.html: programs that read a FASTQ and report Q30, GC content, duplication, insert size and adapter contamination. fastp also trims; MultiQC merges many reports into one page.
one difference from the reference book.
one letter swapped. chr15:100 A>G = at position 100, reference has A, this person has G.
a few letters inserted or deleted. CT>C = one T deleted.
REF = what the reference book says. ALT = what this person has.
the position number on the chromosome.
the 4 things that uniquely name a variant. ("chr15", 40000000, "C", "T").
the SAME deletion can be written several ways. Normalization forces one standard spelling.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: deleting a T from AAAT can be written as position 1 AAAT>AAA or position 4 AT>A. Same biology, different text. If you spell it differently than the answer key, the computer says WRONG.

blocks.text:
The child lost one A from a run of three:

reference   pos: 100 101 102 103
                  A   A   A   T
patient           A   A       T      (one A gone - but WHICH A? nobody can tell)

three legal ways to write the exact same event:
    pos=100  REF=AA  ALT=A      <- leftmost, shortest   (the standard)
    pos=101  REF=AA  ALT=A
    pos=102  REF=AT  ALT=T

  answer key holds : chr15  100  AA  A
  you submit       : chr15  101  AA  A
  scorer compares  : ("chr15",100,"AA","A")  vs  ("chr15",101,"AA","A")
  result           : MISS.  Same biology. Different text. Zero points.
blocks.legendHtml: the three indented lines are the same deletion written three legal ways · only the first survives bcftools norm · the bottom block is what the scorer actually compares.

blocks.html: bcftools norm -f GRCh38.fa -m -both forces the leftmost/shortest spelling on everything. Run it before anything else.
one position where the person has two different ALTs. Splitting (-m -both) breaks it into separate lines.
the doctor-style way to write a variant. NM_001211.6:c.1288A>T or p.Arg430Ter. Different notation from VCF, needs conversion.
a BIG change: a whole chunk deleted, duplicated, flipped, or moved.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: an entire exon of 200 letters gone. A normal SNV caller misses this completely. Callers: Manta, Delly, smoove/LUMPY, GRIDSS.

blocks.html: you have 1 or 3 copies of a chunk instead of 2. Found by depth: half the reads = one copy missing.

blocks.legendHtml: letters shown as . were removed · the size column is how many letters the change spans · the last column is which tool can even see it.

blocks.html: The easy classes are already in the VCF. The hidden second allele is almost certainly one of the hard rows.
a short pattern repeated too many times. CAGCAGCAG... x 200.
a jumping piece of DNA landed in a gene.
what fraction of your reads show the ALT letter.
blocks.exampleHtml: Normal expectations: 0% = you don't have it, ~50% = one copy (het), ~100% = both copies (hom).

blocks.html: the variant is only in SOME of your cells, not all. So VAF comes out weird, like 12%.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: a mistake happened after you were an embryo, so only some cells carry it. Standard callers assume 0/50/100% and throw 12% away as noise.

blocks.html: deliberately hunting for those weird-fraction variants that got thrown away.

the average VAF across all the heterozygous calls on a chromosome. Should sit at 0.5. It is a free whole-chromosome copy-number test: if a fraction of cells carry an extra copy, the average drifts off 0.5 and the depth drifts up.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: measured 0.472–0.497 on every autosome here — flat. That is how we know no mosaic aneuploidy is visible in this blood sample, without aligning a single read. It bounds the aneuploid fraction below roughly 10–15%; it does not disprove the diagnosis, because MVA is diagnosed on cultured cells, not blood.

blocks.text:
30 reads stacked on one position. How many show the ALT letter?

  not present    0/30   |                              |    0%   nothing there
  MOSAIC         4/30   |####                          |   13%   <-- REAL, but the
                                                                      caller deletes it
                                                                      as "noise"
  het           15/30   |###############               |   50%   1 of your 2 copies
  hom           30/30   |##############################|  100%   both copies
blocks.legendHtml: bar length = the fraction of reads carrying the ALT letter · the 13% row is real biology that a standard caller throws away as noise.

blocks.html: Every standard caller assumes only 0% / 50% / 100% exist. MVA is a mosaicism disease — so the 13% row is exactly where a missed allele hides.
how many copies you carry. Het (heterozygous) = 1 of 2 copies changed. Hom (homozygous) = both copies changed. Hemizygous = only 1 copy exists at all (like a boy's X chromosome).

two INFO counters the caller writes on every record. AN = how many copies were looked at in total across all samples; AC = how many of them carried the ALT letter. Software analogy: a numerator and a denominator shipped separately so nobody has to trust a pre-divided float.
blocks.exampleHtml: With one sample AN is always 2 (you have two copies of each autosome), so AC can only be 1 or 2: AC=1 is a het call, AC=2 a hom-alt call. That is why the callset's own INFO/AF (= AC/AN) is only ever 0.5 or 1.0 and says nothing about the population — see the AF trap under gnomAD's AF. Measured in this callset: 3,180,797 alleles at AC=1 and 1,898,267 at AC=2 (methodology 045).

blocks.html: an allele seen exactly once in the whole cohort, i.e. AC=1. Not to be confused with singleton sequencing, which means only the child was sequenced. Both words appear in this project and they mean different things: this case is a sequencing singleton, and in a sequencing singleton every het call is also an allele singleton, which is what collapses bcftools' SiS section into "the het half of the callset".
variant you were born with, in every cell. Somatic — acquired later, in some cells only (cancer works this way).

blocks.alt: Germline is in every cell, mosaic is only in some
blocks.legendHtml: each circle is one cell of the body · red: carries the variant · white: does not.

blocks.html: the caller's confidence numbers. A low GQ het is not proof of absence — look again.
the aligner slightly prefers reads that match the reference, so ALT counts run a bit low.

a count of every kind of letter swap: how many A>G, how many C>T, and so on. Twelve possible swaps, so twelve bars. It is a fingerprint of how the DNA changed, and real biology has a very lopsided one.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: C>T and T>C dominate real human variation, because a chemically tagged C decays into T on its own all the time. Sequencing errors have no such preference — so a spectrum where all twelve bars are the same height is a callset full of artifacts.

blocks.html: DNA has two strands that mirror each other, so the same event reads as G>A from one side and C>T from the other. Collapsing folds each swap together with its mirror image, turning twelve bars into six. Standard in mutational-signature work (COSMIC).
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: G>A counted separately from C>T splits one real signal in half and makes it look weaker than it is.

blocks.html: how many indels of each length, from a single letter up to tens. Deletions plotted as negative, insertions as positive.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ±1 letter dwarfs everything else, so the count axis has to be logarithmic. Whether the length divides by three matters enormously — see frameshift.

blocks.html: variants called per megabase (million letters). Raw variant counts just track chromosome length and say nothing; dividing by length makes a long chromosome and a short one comparable.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ~1,540 variants per Mb, flat across every chromosome in this dataset. Flat is the expected result and worth confirming.

blocks.html: heterozygous calls divided by homozygous-alternate calls. An outbred person lands around 1.3–2.0.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 1.61 here (3,047,077 het / 1,898,267 hom). A low ratio would mean long stretches where both inherited copies are identical, which would argue for a homozygous answer rather than a compound heterozygote.

blocks.html: a picture of all the chromosomes drawn side by side to scale, used to mark where something sits. The classic cytogenetics figure.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the panel gene map in the exploration report is one — 24 bars, with a diamond at each candidate gene's real coordinates.

blocks.html: parts of the genome that look like each other, so scraps can't be placed confidently. Callers do badly here.

blocks.html: on a normal chromosome (1–22), not X or Y. Boys and girls equally affected.

both copies of the gene are hit. Required for recessive disease.
both copies broken, but by TWO DIFFERENT variants — one inherited from mom, one from dad.

both variants sit on the SAME copy. Your other copy is fine, so you're healthy. Immediately eliminates that pair.

cell division. One cell copies its chromosomes and splits into two identical cells.

having the wrong NUMBER of chromosomes. Trisomy = 3 copies instead of 2. Monosomy = 1 copy. Tetraploidy = everything doubled.
only some of the body's cells have wrong chromosome counts.
each affected cell has a DIFFERENT wrong count. Cell A has 3 copies of chr8, cell B has 1 copy of chr20.

the challenge document says explicitly to treat it as evidence, not background. The catch: gene-ranking tools assume every term describes the patient, so feeding them a parental term is a modelling choice. Run it both ways and report the difference.

the second machine-readable input, beside the VCF: this child's symptoms as eight HPO terms and nothing else — no narrative, no phenopacket. Seven describe the child; the eighth, recurrent spontaneous abortion, describes the parents. the standard tool that does that attaching. Two ways to run it: offline from a downloaded cache (~25 GB, genome-scale), or the REST API at rest.ensembl.org (no download, rate-limited to 55,000 requests/hour, batches of 200 variants — right size for a gene panel).

blocks.html: VEP's answer to "what does this variant do to the gene", as a controlled vocabulary term. stop_gained = creates a premature stop, truncating the protein; missense_variant = swaps one amino acid; intron_variant = lands between exons, usually harmless.

VEP's four-bucket severity rollup of the consequence: HIGH (protein destroyed), MODERATE (protein changed), LOW (protein grazed), MODIFIER (outside the protein — the overwhelming majority). A coarse first filter, not a verdict.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: of the 874 panel alleles, 850 are MODIFIER and only 2 are HIGH+rare or MODERATE+rare.

blocks.html: a variant's public catalogue number in dbSNP (NCBI's registry of every variant ever reported), like rs1801516. The VCF's ID column carries it when the caller recognised the site; . means unregistered. Known rsID ≠ harmless — it only means "seen before". The committed offline fixtures' invented alleles are labelled synthetic-1…synthetic-3 on purpose, so nothing that reads as an rsID can be an invented one.

of all the records in a callset, the share that already carry an rsID. A QC metric, not a biological one: a healthy modern human genome is almost entirely made of variants somebody has already seen, so a low rate means novelty, and novelty in bulk usually means artefacts — or an old dbSNP build behind the ID column. Read it only alongside the population it was measured over: filtering, dropping decoy contigs and restricting to SNVs each move it. Example: this callset reads 87.96% over every delivered record and 93.89% over PASS biallelic SNVs, against a published 99.2% per genome.

one position with exactly one ALT allele, i.e. the opposite of a multiallelic one. Careful: biallelic is used in two unrelated senses in this field. Here it is a property of a VCF row (how many ALTs are on the line); in the recessive-disease sense above it is a property of a gene (both copies hit). Nothing connects them. Example: REF=A ALT=G is a biallelic site; REF=A ALT=G,T is not.

SNV count divided by indel count in one callset. A shape check: substitutions vastly outnumber insertions and deletions, and a ratio that drifts low says the caller is emitting more indels than a reference pipeline would. Strongly caller-dependent — the same reads give 4.7 through DeepVariant and 6.2 through GATK — so it flags a difference, never a defect on its own. Example: 4,086,641 SNPs / 930,181 indels = 4.393 here, against 4.611–4.798 across the 1000G superpopulations.

blocks.html: the 5 verdicts.
"we don't know". Most variants are this.

how a ClinVar verdict was arrived at, not how strong the evidence behind it is. ClinVar renders it as 0–4 stars: ★★★★ practice_guideline (a clinical guideline says so), ★★★ reviewed_by_expert_panel (a curated expert group), ★★ criteria_provided,_multiple_submitters,_no_conflicts (several labs, stated criteria, agreeing), ★ criteria_provided,_single_submitter (one lab, stated criteria), ☆☆☆☆ no_assertion_criteria_provided (somebody asserted it without saying how). Software analogy: a code-review trail, not a test result — it tells you who signed off and under what process, never whether the code works. A separate value, criteria_provided,_conflicting_classifications, means submitters disagree; the P/LP predicate excludes it, because a disagreement is the opposite of an assertion.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: of the 2,129 pathogenic/likely-pathogenic ClinVar records inside the 8-gene panel, 111 are ★★★, 664 ★★, 1,265 ★ and 89 ☆☆☆☆ — nearly six in ten rest on a single submitter (methodology 051).

blocks.html: ClinVar's own stable key for a record, e.g. 533901. Use it rather than the rsID: 4,442 of the 17,832 rows in our committed ClinVar extract have no rsID at all, and every one has a Variation ID. Resolvable at ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/variation/<id>/.

running the ClinVar join backwards: instead of taking a variant the callset produced and asking what is known about it, take every site already classified pathogenic and ask whether the callset contains it. Both outcomes are results — a known-pathogenic site called heterozygous is a direct lead, and a gene whose known pathogenic sites are all absent says the case is not a repeat of a previously published family. The catch is spelling: an exact-string match under-counts indels unless both sides are left-aligned first, so a presence count is a lower bound, never a ceiling.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 2,129 pathogenic/likely-pathogenic panel sites checked, 1 present — the BUB1B stop_gained, heterozygous and PASS — with 1,306 of the 2,129 indel-shaped and therefore subject to the spelling caveat (methodology 051).

what fraction of people carry it. popmax = the highest frequency in any single population group (safer than the global average); gnomAD v4 renamed it grpmax.
blocks.exampleHtml: Two different fields share this name and only one of them is a population frequency. The gnomAD AF is. The INFO/AF inside our own VCF is not — it is AC/AN computed within the sample, so with one sample it is only ever 0.5 or 1.0. Same field name, same column header in bcftools stats, completely different meaning; filtering on the wrong one silently throws away real candidates. The measured consequence is data-findings §2.5. Logic here: MVA has under 50 patients worldwide, so a causing variant must be super rare. But the cut-off depends on inheritance: the literature uses AF < 1e-3 (0.1%) for dominant disease and AF < 1e-2 (1%) for recessive and compound-het — healthy carriers keep a recessive allele circulating (Pedersen 2021, PMID 34267211; Whiffin 2017, PMID 28518168). Filtering compound-het candidates at 1e-3 silently drops real alleles sitting between 0.1% and 1%. The thresholds live in ressources/reference/qc_norms.tsv.

blocks.html: measures whether a gene tolerates being broken in healthy people.
blocks.exampleHtml: High pLI = nobody healthy has a broken copy = breaking it is probably serious. The recessive trap: gnomAD is full of healthy carriers of recessive disease alleles, so recessive-disease genes score as tolerant. Measured on our panel: BUB1B pLI = 2.6e-14 and CEP57 pLI = 6.8e-06 — the two established MVA genes look completely unconstrained. Never rank recessive candidates by constraint; show it only as context (methodology 030).

blocks.html: one giant pre-computed table with dozens of prediction scores already joined together. Saves days.
more variant databases (disease variants, structural variants, patient cases).

blocks.term: PubMed / Europe PMC / PubTator3 / LitVar2 / OpenAlex / Semantic Scholar
blocks.html: ways to search scientific papers by program instead of by hand. PubTator3 already tags which genes and variants each paper mentions.
the ID number of a paper. Every claim must carry one, or it can't be checked.

a paper describing one real patient: their symptoms, the variants found, how it was confirmed. For an ultra-rare disease the world's knowledge is mostly case reports — and a validated challenge case may itself have been published as one. Example: "Compound heterozygous BUB1B variants in a child with MVA and rhabdomyosarcoma" would be a direct answer-key candidate.
databases of which proteins talk to which, and which drugs hit which target.
3D shapes and facts about proteins. Lets you see where in the protein your variant lands. Each is defined properly in §9: AlphaFold, pLDDT, mmCIF, UniProt accession.
drug databases. Needed for Track 2.
public genomes from healthy volunteers, free to use. Perfect for testing your pipeline without touching patient data.
writing down exactly which release of each database you used, so results can be reproduced later.

the paper trail behind one number or one file: which tool, at which version, with which settings, reading which inputs, produced it. It is what makes a result checkable by someone who was not there. The rule this project holds itself to is that provenance is recorded by the tool that did the work, never typed in afterwards — a paper trail a human can edit is a claim about the past, and a claim is exactly the thing provenance is supposed to replace.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ressources/reference/structure_genes.tsv is 23 gene records; beside it, structure_genes.provenance.json says they were resolved by tools/build_gene_set.py at commit cb066b8 against rest.ensembl.org release 116 on 2026-09-03.
blocks.context: recorded by the tool that did the work, on every run

blocks.html: the table of genes a 3D protein exhibit is allowed to draw a fold for. Deliberately a superset of the genes the patient's variants were annotated against: reading one protein's shape against a related gene's needs that related gene on screen, and it carries no patient variant at all. One row per gene, resolved live against Ensembl by tools/build_gene_set.py and committed, so the offline app and the live server read the same list. Compare the panel, which is the smaller, annotation-defined set.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ressources/reference/structure_genes.tsv — 23 genes, of which 8 are the annotated panel, 5 are other documented MVA / spindle-checkpoint genes and 10 are comparison requests.

blocks.html: how a reference table tells the app to arrange its rows, as opposed to what it claims about them. Three fields on every row: an opaque short id (panel), the sentence a heading shows (annotated panel (alleles painted)), and the group's rank, which also decides its colour. The point is that the id is free-form — no code anywhere lists the groups — so another project renames and re-ranks every group by editing one TSV. A display group carries no claim about evidence or about the patient; the flag that does is in_panel.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: rank 0 is drawn in the "goal" green and rank 1 in blue, so renaming mva-sac to spindle-checkpoint changes every heading and keeps every colour.

blocks.html: the Swiss-army knives for VCF and BAM files. bcftools norm, bcftools view, bcftools stats.
measures coverage fast.
a picture viewer for reads. You look at the actual scraps stacked over a position and judge with your eyes. igv.js / igv-reports = the shareable web version.
draws pictures of structural variants.

blocks.term: Exomiser / LIRICAL / AMELIE / Phen2Gene / GADO / Phenolyzer
blocks.html: programs that take the symptom list + the VCF and rank which gene is guilty.
blocks.exampleHtml: Exomiser and LIRICAL are Java; Phen2Gene is Python and also answers over HTTP; Phenolyzer is Perl. We reimplemented the phenotype half in Python — see the four entries below.

blocks.html: measuring how alike two symptom lists are by walking the ontology, never by comparing the words. "Rhabdomyosarcoma" and "nephroblastoma" share no letters and are one step apart in the graph.
of all the terms two symptoms both descend from, the rarest one. That term's information content is their similarity score. This is Resnik similarity.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Rhabdomyosarcoma and Nephroblastoma meet at "Neoplasm", which is informative. Rhabdomyosarcoma and Premature birth meet near the root, which is worth nothing.

blocks.html: how you go from comparing two terms to comparing two lists. Each term takes its single strongest partner on the other side; those bests are averaged. Taking the best lets a real match survive six unrelated symptoms; averaging stops one lucky pairing carrying the whole score.
blocks.exampleHtml: Software analogy: a fuzzy join where every left row keeps only its best right match, then you average the match qualities.

blocks.html: BMA is not symmetric, and both halves are misleading alone. Forward asks "is each of the child's features explained by this gene?" and ignores everything else the gene does. Reverse asks "is each of the gene's features present in the child?" and punishes well-studied genes for the symptoms the child lacks. Report both; their gap says how heavily the gene is curated, not anything about the patient.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: BUB1B has 112 curated features against this child's 7 — forward 2.11, reverse 0.55.

blocks.html: the published scoring scheme built from MICA + BMA, normalised so a perfect match is 1.0. What Exomiser's phenotype scoring is made of.

Exomiser's phenotype scorers. PHIVE uses mouse models, PhenIX human disease annotations only, hiPHIVE combines human + mouse + zebrafish + a protein-interaction network. Counter-intuitively, hiPHIVE restricted to human only beats the full cross-species version: 82.8% vs 66.6% top-10 (Genome Medicine vol 17 art 127, 2025). That finding is why a Python reimplementation is practical at all — the parts that are hard to rebuild are the parts to leave out.

the embedded Java database format Exomiser ships its data in. No Python reader exists, which is what makes Exomiser's variant half genuinely Java-only. Its phenotype inputs (hp.obo, genes_to_phenotype.txt) are plain text and readable by anything.
a numeric gene identifier, e.g. 701 for BUB1B. An alternative to the HGNC symbol. Ours joins on symbols because that is what VEP returns; the numeric id is kept only because some services key on it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Gotcha: 375 rows of HPO's gene file carry - as the symbol, covering seven different genes. Loading them creates one fake gene that outranks real ones.

blocks.html: a per-gene multiplier applied to a candidate pair's score. A hand-set prior ("BUB1B matters, multiply by 2") is an assumption and our register logs it as evidence of strength zero. A prior derived from a phenotype ranking over 5,267 genes is a measurement, and can carry real weight.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: BUB1B ranks 6 of 5,267 on this child's symptoms, giving a prior of 1.455.

blocks.html: filter VCFs with written rules, including compound-het logic.
turns bcftools stats output into charts: variant classes, substitution spectrum, indel length spectrum, depth. The reference for what a callset overview should show.

a charting library whose figures are interactive in a plain HTML file: zoom, hover for exact values, toggle a series off. No server and no build step, which is why MultiQC and this repository's exploration report both use it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: uv run mva-explore report ressources/data-profile writes one such page — see the exploration toolkit.

blocks.html: the language that says how a web page looks: one rule per selector, each setting properties like color or padding. The browser applies every matching rule and the most specific one wins.

a styling library where you never write a CSS rule; you put pre-made single-purpose class names on the element instead (p-4 = padding 4, text-sm = small text). The build step scans your source text for class names and emits only the rules you actually used. That scan is the catch worth knowing: a class name assembled at runtime (`bg-${colour}`) is never seen, so its rule is never generated and the style silently does nothing.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: <div className="rounded-xl border border-chrome-800 p-4"> — four utility classes instead of one hand-written CSS rule.

blocks.html: one of those single-purpose class names. A recipe in this repository is a named string of them (CARD = 'rounded-xl border border-chrome-800 bg-chrome-900/40 p-4') so eleven files stop retyping the same eight words. Example: app/src/lib/ui.ts.

a value declared once under a name starting with -- and read anywhere with var(--name). It lives in the browser, so it can be swapped at runtime; a value baked into a JavaScript file cannot. Example: --color-good-500: #00c950; then color: var(--color-good-500).

a text-to-diagram language: you write the boxes and arrows as words in a fenced ```mermaid block and a renderer draws them. GitHub, VS Code and this project's /learn page draw them; a plain text editor shows the source, which is why every diagram here also has a > **Legend** line that reads without the picture. Example: flowchart LR; A --> B draws two boxes with an arrow.

a named design value used instead of a literal one: a colour, a spacing, a radius. Software analogy: a constant, except it has to be readable from both CSS and code, which is why it usually exists twice. Example: --color-broken-400 and RAMP.broken[400] are the same token in this repository's two halves.

a colour written as #RRGGBB, two hex digits per red/green/blue channel, in the sRGB space every screen understands. Eight digits add an alpha (opacity) channel. Example: #00c950 = the app's "good" green; #1c398e55 = a blue at ~33 % opacity.

a newer way to write a colour, as lightness, chroma (how vivid), hue (which colour) in a space built so equal numeric steps look like equal steps to the eye — unlike hex, where lightening a colour by hand shifts its hue. Tailwind v4 ships its palette in oklch. Converting it to hex is lossy at the edges (some oklch colours are outside sRGB and get clipped) but necessary for anything that parses colours itself, such as Plotly.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: oklch(72.3% 0.219 149.579) is Tailwind's green-500, which converts to #00c950.

blocks.html: a hue ramp named for what it means rather than what it is: this repository paints with good (green), broken (red), decision (yellow), machinery (blue), raw (purple), chrome (grey furniture) and severity (orange). The Tailwind hue each is cut from appears in one generator script and nowhere else, so renaming the meaning never means editing 900 call sites. Example: bg-good-950 rather than bg-emerald-950.

one step on a family, numbered 50 (palest) to 950 (deepest). This repository uses 300/400 for text, 800/900 for borders and 950 for a tinted background, so a new family has an obvious answer for every role. Example: text-broken-400 on bg-broken-950.

the six meanings a component is allowed to be tinted with: neutral, good, broken, decision, machinery, raw. A component takes a tone, never a semantic colour family and never a hex — which is what stops a badge and the number above it from disagreeing about what green means. Example: <Badge tone="decision">gap</Badge>.

a list of [position, colour] stops between 0 and 1 that a chart interpolates to colour a continuous range. Sequential runs dark → hot; diverging puts a distinct colour at each end and a neutral one in the middle, for a value whose direction of deviation matters. Example: this repository's allele-balance scale puts green at 0.5 — the middle is the goal — with red below and purple above.
Python libraries to read these files in code.

a database that runs inside your program, as a library, with the whole database in a single file. There is no server process, no port and no database accounts — the same arrangement as SQLite, but column-oriented and built for analytics. This is the single most commonly misunderstood thing about it: you cannot "expose DuckDB on a server", because there is nothing listening. Putting it on a shared machine means putting the file there and reaching it the way you already reach that machine.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: duckdb profile.duckdb "SELECT * FROM panel_variant_counts" — the binary opens the file, answers, and exits.

blocks.html: a database that is a library linked into your process rather than a service you connect to. The opposite is a client–server database (PostgreSQL, MySQL), where a long-running daemon owns the data and clients talk to it over a socket. Embedded means zero setup and no network attack surface; it also means one writer at a time, because the lock is a file lock. DuckDB and SQLite are embedded; Postgres is not.

a file format that stores tables by column rather than by row, so scanning one column of millions of rows never reads the others. It also carries its own schema, so the column types survive the trip; a TSV does not, which is why a number written to a TSV comes back as text unless something re-infers it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: vcf_chrom_allele_balance.parquet — 24 rows, 1.3 KB, and mean_dp is a DOUBLE on the way out because it was one on the way in.

blocks.html: the horizontal slice a Parquet file is built from: a block of rows whose columns are compressed and indexed together, with the minimum and maximum of each column recorded in the footer. Those min/max statistics are what lets a reader skip a whole block without reading it, and the reason sorting a file by the column you filter on makes it dramatically cheaper to query. The group is also the writer's buffer — it holds a full group in memory before flushing it — so the size you choose is a direct memory cost.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: 1,000,000 rows per group, so a read store shard of 4M reads has 4 skippable blocks.

blocks.html: one file of a table that is deliberately split across many files, rather than one enormous file. Splitting buys parallelism (readers take a file each) and pruning (a query that only concerns lane 1 never opens the others). Hive partitioning is the convention that puts the partitioning column in the directory name — lane=1/read=2/part-0007.parquet — so the value is readable without opening the file, and query engines turn a WHERE lane = 1 into "open only that directory".
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: s3://mva/reads/lane=3/read=1/part-0012.parquet.

blocks.html: a standard layout for a table in memory, column by column. Its point is that two programs agreeing on it can hand a table to each other with no conversion and no copying: a Rust library can produce reads and DuckDB can query them in place. Parquet is the on-disk form of the same idea; Arrow is the in-memory one.

a chunk of an Arrow table, a few thousand rows at a time. Reading a file as a stream of batches is what makes a converter's memory bounded by the batch size rather than by the file size — the difference between converting an 11 GB FASTQ and running out of RAM trying.

Rust libraries for reading bioinformatics file formats. noodles is the parser itself; oxbow and polars-bio wrap it and hand the result out as Arrow batches, which is what makes them usable from Python without a per-record Python loop. This repository uses oxbow to convert FASTQ to Parquet, measured at ~854,000 reads/second versus ~50,000 for a shell pipeline (methodology 018).

reading the first rows of a text table to guess each column's type. DuckDB's CSV reader does this; mva-warehouse leans on it deliberately rather than hand-rolling a guesser, so the staging step and an analyst's own read_csv can never disagree.

one queryable copy of derived tables, kept apart from the raw data they came from. Here it is deliberately small: the profile tables, typed and joinable, on a machine the team shares. It is a derived dataset — rebuildable at any time, and therefore safe to delete.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: uv run mva-warehouse pg-ingest — see the infrastructure runbook.

blocks.html: a named group of tables inside one database, the way a package groups modules in code. A table's full address is <schema>.<table>, and two schemas can hold different tables with the same name. This warehouse uses exactly two: warehouse for ingested data and the hand-written append-only ledgers, and results for everything computed from them. The split is load-bearing — re-ingesting cannot destroy a derived table, and re-deriving cannot corrupt an input.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: warehouse.variants_raw is the delivered callset; results.contig_density is a table computed from it.

blocks.html: a set of read-only views every SQL database exposes describing itself: which tables exist, which columns each has, and what type each column is. It is how a catalogue can list a database it was never told about. What it cannot supply is meaning — it knows mean_vaf is a floating-point number, not that 0.50 is the value a healthy diploid genome gives, which is why that sentence has to be written down in code.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: /api/catalog/columns reads it live and returns 262 rows, one per column of the 38 tables.

blocks.html: the mainstream open-source client–server database. A daemon owns the data; clients connect over a socket, authenticate, and many can read and write at the same time. Row-oriented, so it is slower than a column store for wide analytical scans — but that is not what you ask it for. Use it for the things that change: a ledger, a results table, anything several people append to.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: measured on 5,012,204 variant records — 653 MB in Postgres versus 17 MB as Parquet, and 287 ms versus 18 ms on the same filter query.

blocks.html: the restriction that only one process may hold an embedded database file open. In DuckDB it is stricter than it sounds: a held write lock blocks readers as well, so one long write makes the file unreadable for everyone. This, not speed, is the reason a shared team store needs a real server.
pointing DuckDB at another database so its tables appear alongside your own, queryable in one statement. This is how DuckDB acts as an engine over Postgres rather than a replacement for it.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ATTACH 'host=box dbname=mva' AS pg (TYPE postgres); then CREATE TABLE pg.results AS SELECT … FROM read_parquet('variants.parquet') — DuckDB does the scan, Postgres keeps the answer.

blocks.html: a lakehouse format from the DuckDB project: the data stays as Parquet files, while the catalog (which files make up which table, and at which version) lives in a real database such as Postgres. That split buys concurrent writers and time travel without giving up columnar speed.
the bookkeeping that says which files constitute which table. Keeping it in a transactional database is what lets several writers agree on what the table currently is.

querying a table as it was at an earlier version, because every change was recorded as a snapshot instead of overwriting. Useful well beyond undo: it is an audit trail, which is what a scientific result needs when someone asks which version of the candidate table produced a submission.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: SELECT count(*) FROM lake.panel AT (VERSION => 1) returned 8 while the live table held 9.

blocks.html: whether a table is laid out one record at a time or one column at a time. A row store fetches a whole record cheaply, which suits transactions; a column store reads one field across millions of records without touching the others, which suits analytics. Postgres is the former, DuckDB and Parquet the latter — the reason both appear in this design rather than one winning.

the one copy everything else is derived from, kept unchanged on purpose. Here it is the delivered files in object storage: no parsing, no filtering, no typing. Anything wrong downstream can be rebuilt from it; it can never be rebuilt from anything else.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: s3://mva/source/ holds all 12 delivered files, 84.99 GB, byte-for-byte as published.

blocks.html: a short fingerprint computed from every byte of a file. Two files with the same SHA-256 are the same file; change one bit and the fingerprint changes completely. It is how you prove a transfer did not corrupt anything.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the delivered VCF is bec64c68d3ad10d0…, and the publisher says the same, so our copy is the delivery.

blocks.html: a Git extension that keeps big files outside the repository and leaves a pointer behind. It records a real SHA-256 for each stored file; ordinary Git objects instead carry a 40-character blob SHA-1, computed over different bytes with a different algorithm. Comparing one against the other produces a mismatch that means nothing.

a store setting where writing to an existing key creates a new version beside the old one instead of replacing it. It makes an accidental overwrite recoverable, which is what turns "we keep the raw data" into something that survives a mistake.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the VCF was uploaded twice — from a laptop, then re-fetched on the server — and MinIO holds both versions.

blocks.html: the record of which inputs produced which table, by which transformation. Not "it came from a VCF", but which object, at which version, with which checksum, producing how many rows. Without it, a disputed result cannot be traced back. Stored as an append-only edge list: one row per (input → output) pair.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: warehouse.data_lineage links variants_raw to s3://mva/source/WGS_EX2312012_HGWCNDSX7.vcf.gz, sha256 bec64c68…, version 3a79ea8b…, 5,012,204 rows.
blocks.context: the graph behind every derived table in the warehouse

blocks.html: one row of that record: one output table, one input, one transformation. A derived table with no edge is a table nobody can vouch for. Read the edges with mva-warehouse lineage-list.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: results.panel_gene_density ← warehouse.panel_variant_counts, warehouse.mva_panel_grch38, tool mva-warehouse pg-derive.
blocks.context: eleven stored columns — produced_at, target_schema, target_table, target_rows, source_kind, source_ref, source_version, source_sha256, transform, tool, notes — plus is_current, computed on read and never stored, because a stored flag would mean updating a table whose whole value is that it is never updated

blocks.html: a small file committed beside a data file, saying where that file came from. It is what you write when there is nothing to derive: a public reference table, an ontology release, a gene record, a predicted protein structure are all fetched, not computed, so there is no input table and no transformation and a lineage edge for them would be invented. The manifest names the upstream URL and its release instead, the checksum of every input read and every output written, the tool, and the commit it ran at. Written by that tool on every run.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: ressources/reference/hpo_provenance.json and app/src/fixtures/data/protein/_provenance.json; GET /api/provenance/reference lists every one of them in a single row shape.

blocks.html: the same question at two grains, and the words are not interchangeable. Lineage is an edge in a graph: this table came from that object by that transform, and it only exists where something was derived. Provenance is the whole paper trail for one artefact, derived or not — which is why fetched reference data has a provenance manifest and no lineage edge. Every lineage edge is provenance; not all provenance is lineage.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: warehouse.hpo_gene_scores has both — a data_lineage edge saying the staged Parquet produced it, and hpo_provenance.json saying which HPO release the Parquet was computed from. The AlphaFold trace behind a protein exhibit has only the second.

blocks.html: how an append-only table is corrected: you append a newer row and say in its notes which earlier row it replaces. The wrong row stays, because the fact that the claim changed is itself evidence. Updating in place would destroy that.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: the first variants_raw edge named a laptop path with no checksum; the superseding edge names the verified object in the bucket and carries supersedes the edge produced at 2026-08-29 16:37:29.

blocks.html: a table that only ever gains rows; nothing is edited or deleted. Used where the history is the point, such as an upload ledger or a lineage log. A record that can be quietly rewritten is not evidence.
the first place data arrives, stored in its delivered form before anything is interpreted. Separating it from the typed, queryable layer means a parsing mistake is always recoverable.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: warehouse.variants_raw — one row per VCF line, every field text, nothing filtered.

blocks.html: a copy tool that transfers only the parts of a file that changed, and resumes where it left off. The right way to move a directory to a remote box repeatedly; scp re-sends everything every time.

an operation that gives the same result whether you run it once or five times. An upload that lands the same file twice records both attempts in the ledger but leaves one object in the store, so repeating it is safe. mva-warehouse stage is idempotent too: it rewrites build/warehouse/*.parquet from the profile directory, so running it twice costs time and changes nothing.
the language for asking a database questions.
tools that chain all the steps into one reproducible command.
a frozen box holding your exact software versions, so it runs the same everywhere.
a request a service answers about itself: "am I running?" It touches nothing, so it answers in microseconds. What a container orchestrator asks before deciding to restart a process.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: GET /health on this project's API → {"ok": true, "service": "mva-viz-api"} — true even if the database behind it is dead.

blocks.html: the harder question the liveness probe cannot answer: "is everything I need working?" One check per backend, each doing the cheapest real thing that proves it — a SELECT 1 on the database, one capped listing on the object store, one row read through the Parquet path. A dead backend becomes a down row in the answer, never an error, so the page reporting it can never itself be the thing that broke.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: GET /api/health/dependencies → seven rows; the Status page draws one card each.

blocks.html: how long one check may take before it is declared down. It has to match what that check actually does: a database greet over the network is not a ping to the local process. Too short and a slow-but-alive service is reported as an outage, which sends a developer to fix something that was never broken.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: reference-snapshots counts rows in two ingested reference tables and measured 1,934 ms, then 2,134 ms, then 3.1 s on the same healthy database — so its budget is 15 s, while the API's self-check keeps 2 s (methodology 065).

blocks.html: replacing a value with a marker ([redacted], ••••) instead of showing it. Two different uses in this project, worth keeping apart: the API always scrubs credentials out of any text it returns, which is a hard rule; the Status page additionally hides hosts and ports until asked, which is presentation hygiene for a screenshot — the values are still in the response, so it prevents an accidental display, not access.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: mva@db.example:5432/mva renders as ••••@••••:••••/mva until you press show.

blocks.html: a cloud service to rent CPUs/GPUs for the heavy steps.
big-data machinery, useful for thousands of patients, pointless for one.
compare two VCFs to score how well you called variants.
check the sample isn't contaminated and that all the files really come from the same person.
every possible chunk of length k from a sequence. k=31 means every 31-letter window.

blocks.term: Mapping-free / alignment-free k-mer scan (MALVA, jellyfish, SKA2)
blocks.html: search the raw FASTQ for a specific 31-letter fingerprint directly, skipping the whole align-and-call pipeline. Minutes instead of a day.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: you know exactly what a published BUB1B variant looks like. Build its fingerprint, count how many raw scraps contain it. Done.

blocks.html: search text for a pattern. The simplest possible tool, and often enough.
a plain list of genome regions (chromosome, start, end). Used to say "only look here".

Ensembl's gene-model file: one tab-separated line per gene, transcript, exon, CDS or stop codon, with a semicolon-packed attribute column (gene_id "…"; gene_name "…"; transcript_biotype "…";). It is the coordinate source for "which bases are coding". Like a BED with a type column and a bag of key–value tags.
blocks.exampleHtml: Example: Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.116.gtf.gz, 141 MB, ~11 million lines, 2,977,130 of them CDS or stop-codon rows of protein-coding transcripts — the input to tools/build_coding_regions.py.

chapters.title: Prediction scores (guessing if a variant is harmful)

blocks.html: a computer's guess, no lab experiment. ("in silico" = in the chip.)

blocks.alt: Which predictor can see which class of variant
blocks.legendHtml: green: the tool handles that class · yellow: only partly · red: blind to it · the red dashed box is the zone no effect predictor covers.

blocks.html: a variant that swaps one amino acid for another. Hardest class to judge: sometimes fatal, usually harmless.
a genome-wide "how bad does this look" score. Works on everything, but only roughly.
missense-only scores built by combining other scores.
DeepMind's missense score. Strong.
models that learned protein language from millions of natural proteins, then judge whether your change "sounds wrong". They never saw ClinVar, which is an advantage (see circularity).
predict whether a variant wrecks splicing. Critical here, because a leaky splice variant is the most likely hidden second allele.
blocks.exampleHtml: ±1000 nt window = how far from the exon SpliceAI is allowed to look. The default ±50 is too narrow and misses deep-intronic answers.

blocks.text:
<------------ intron ------------>[  EXON  ]<--- intron --->
                          X                                          X = the real variant,
                                                                         300 letters deep
   default +/- 50 nt                  [~~~~~~~~~~~~~~]      variant NOT in the window -> missed
   wide    +/- 1000 nt   [~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~] variant IS in the window  -> caught
blocks.legendHtml: [ EXON ] is the exon · ~~~ marks how far the model is allowed to look · X is the variant · at the default window it falls outside and is never scored.

blocks.html: scores for non-coding variants. Noisy; only trust inside a gene you already suspect.
huge new models that read a big stretch of DNA and predict what it does. Powerful, uncalibrated, expensive.
sanity-check whether a "loss of function" variant really destroys the protein.
has this exact letter stayed unchanged across many species for millions of years? If yes, it probably matters.
the model was never trained on this task, it just knows enough to answer anyway.
the model's score, in log form. Bigger = more surprising = more likely damaging.
the score orders things correctly but the number itself is not a real probability. "0.8" doesn't mean 80%.

blocks.term: Domain database (Pfam, SMART, PROSITE, Gene3D, SUPERFAMILY, CDD, PRINTS)
aliases: Pfam, SMART, PROSITE, Gene3D, SUPERFAMILY, CDD, PRINTS
blocks.html: seven independent catalogues that each scan a protein sequence and call out the domains they recognise. They overlap on purpose: the same region called by four of them is agreement, not duplication. InterPro is the umbrella that maps their accessions onto one shared id. Example: BUBR1's N-terminal region is PF08311 to Pfam, SM00777 to SMART and PS51489 to PROSITE — all three IPR013212 in InterPro. Ensembl serves them from /overlap/translation/<protein id>, mixed in with things that are not domains (PDB cross-references, AlphaFold models, disorder and coiled-coil predictions), so the list has to be filtered.

the standard way to draw variants against a protein: the x axis is amino-acid position, domains are bars along it, and each variant is a stem with a coloured head at its position. It answers "does this change hit a working part?" — the question a genomic coordinate cannot.

which bead in the chain a variant changes, counted from 1. VEP reports it per transcript, and it is absent for anything outside the coding sequence — an intronic or splice-region change has no amino acid to name. Example: a missense_variant at protein_start: 349 swaps bead 349.

the stable ID of a protein sequence in UniProt, the reference catalogue of proteins. Same idea as an Ensembl gene ID, one level down the chain: a gene ID names the recipe, a translation ID (ENSP…) names one gene's protein in Ensembl's own numbering, and a UniProt accession names that protein in the numbering the rest of the protein world uses. Six or ten characters, letters and digits. Structure databases are keyed by it, so it is the join key you need before you can ask for a shape. Example: BUB1B's protein is ENSP00000287598 to Ensembl and O60566 to UniProt — the same 1050 beads, two id systems. Ensembl translates between them at /xrefs/id/<ENSP>?external_db=Uniprot/SWISSPROT, whose primary_id is the accession. Watch out: the neighbouring display_id is O60566.231, an accession plus a sequence version, and it 404s against a structure database.

the one carbon atom every amino acid has in the same place, in the middle of the bead. Chain them and you get the backbone: the protein's spine, as a path through space. A full protein is ~8,000 atoms; its alpha carbons are ~1,000 points, one per bead. That is a ~90 % saving for no loss of the thing you actually want to see, which is the overall fold and how far apart two beads are. Example: BUBR1's Cα trace is 1,050 points; residue 1's is at (27.21, 69.68, 11.46) ångström (Å, a ten-billionth of a metre — the unit atoms are measured in). Two Cα atoms within ~8 Å are touching in space, however far apart they are along the sequence.

the unit every atomic coordinate in a structure file is written in: 10⁻¹⁰ m, a ten-billionth of a metre. It exists because metres and nanometres are the wrong size for atoms — in ångström the numbers a reader cares about are single- and double-digit. The three scales worth memorising: a chemical bond is ~1.5 Å, two consecutive alpha carbons are ~3.8 Å apart, and a whole protein domain is ~30–40 Å across. Example: BUBR1's Cα for residue 1 sits at (27.21, 69.68, 11.46) Å in the model's own frame — an arbitrary origin, so only differences between two points mean anything, never a single coordinate.

the straight-line distance between two residues' alpha carbons, in ångström. It is the one number that answers "are these two changes hitting the same place?", and it is the reason a 3D view earns its place over a lollipop plot: a protein folds, so distance along the sequence is a poor proxy for distance in space. Two residues 300 amino acids apart on the chain can pack into one pocket, and two neighbours on the chain can point at opposite faces. Read it as a geometric band, not a verdict: under ~10 Å the two residues could share one binding pocket, 10–25 Å puts them in the same lobe of the fold, and beyond ~25 Å they are separate sites. Two caveats ride with every number: on an AlphaFold model a distance is only as good as the pLDDT at both ends (below 70 it is not quotable), and a short distance is a mechanism hypothesis, never a demonstration that either change breaks the other's function. Example: in the app's protein exhibit the picked pair is drawn as a line labelled 12.3 Å.

the two local shapes a stretch of backbone repeatedly folds into: an alpha helix (a corkscrew) and a beta strand (a flat extended piece; several side by side make a sheet). Everything else is coil or loop. It is the layer between the bare sequence (primary structure) and the whole 3D fold (tertiary structure) — think of it as the paragraph structure of the protein. Useful because a variant in the middle of a helix and one in a floppy loop are different risks. Example: residues 4–23 of BUBR1 are a helix; 1–2 are a strand. Absence of an annotation means not annotated, never "all coil" — a file that carries no secondary-structure table is silent, not flat.

DeepMind's neural network that predicts a protein's 3D shape from its amino-acid sequence alone, and AlphaFold DB (alphafold.ebi.ac.uk) the free database of its predictions for essentially every known protein. It exists because measuring a real structure in a lab takes months per protein, and most proteins have never been measured. The word to keep in front of you is prediction: an AlphaFold model is a hypothesis about shape, and quoting one as if it were a measurement is a claim you have not earned — which is what pLDDT below is for. Keyed by UniProt accession, returns one entry per isoform, and every model has a version you must read from the reply rather than compose. Example: GET https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/api/prediction/O60566 answers with three isoform models — AF-O60566-F1 (1050 beads), -2-F1 (933), -3-F1 (1064) — each at latestVersion: 6. Picking the wrong one paints bead 349 of your variant onto bead 349 of a different protein. Contrast the PDB (Protein Data Bank), which holds experimentally measured structures — far fewer, usually partial, but measured.

AlphaFold's own confidence in each individual bead's position, 0–100 (the name is "predicted local distance difference test"). It is the honesty channel of a predicted structure, and the numbers have conventional meanings: above 90 the bead's position is reliable to atomic detail; 70–90 the backbone is about right; 50–70 treat with caution; below 50 the region is probably intrinsically disordered — floppy, with no single shape to predict, so the coordinates are close to meaningless. A prediction with low pLDDT is not a broken prediction; it is a correct statement that the answer is unknown, and drawing it in the same colour as a confident region is the mistake. Example: BUBR1's model scores 63.59 overall with 37.3 % of its beads at very-low pLDDT, so more than a third of that protein supports no spatial claim at all. Any exhibit painting it has to show pLDDT, or it is asserting shape it does not have.

the standard text format for 3D structures, and the modern replacement for the old fixed-column PDB format. In software terms: a bundle of CSVs in one file, with named headers. A category is a table; a table with many rows is written as loop_, then one _category.column line per column, then whitespace-separated data rows. The table you want is _atom_site, one row per atom. chapters.title: ACMG — the official way to judge a variant

blocks.html: the rulebook clinical labs use to call a variant pathogenic or not. A checklist of evidence codes.
one piece of evidence with a name and a strength.

• PVS1 — Pathogenic, Very Strong: kills the protein (truncating in a gene where that's the known mechanism).
  • PS3 — Pathogenic Strong: lab experiment proves it's broken.
  • PS4 — Pathogenic Strong: seen much more in patients than in healthy people.
  • PM2 — Pathogenic Moderate: absent from gnomAD (too rare to be harmless).
  • PM3 — Pathogenic Moderate: found in trans with a known pathogenic variant. Compound-het structure is itself evidence.
  • PP3 — Pathogenic Supporting: computer predictors agree it's damaging.
  • PP4 — Pathogenic Supporting: the patient's symptoms match this gene's disease specifically.
  • PP1 — Pathogenic Supporting: tracks with disease through the family.
  • BP4 / BA1 — Benign codes: predictors say harmless / far too common in the population.
turns those codes into numbers you can add up.
blocks.exampleHtml: Supporting = 1 pt, Moderate = 2, Strong = 4, Very Strong = 8; benign codes count negative. Total ≥ 10 → Pathogenic. 6–9 → Likely pathogenic. 0–5 → VUS. ≤ −7 → Benign. Value: one defensible number instead of an argument.

blocks.html: population genetics formula. If a bad allele has frequency q, then q² of people are homozygous for it.

blocks.html: the coin-flip distribution. A true het at 30× depth: alt reads ~ Binomial(30, 0.5). Getting 4 out of 30 would be very odd.

the data varies more than the simple model expects.
distributions for counting things (like reads per bin). Used to spot deletions: half the expected reads = one copy lost.
the boring explanation. "This 5% VAF is just sequencing error." You test whether the data can reject it.
the chance your test would actually detect a real effect. At 30× depth, power to spot a 10% mosaic variant at one site is poor — so restrict the search to one gene.
test 5 million positions and some will look significant by pure luck.

a model for "the truth changes in stretches". Used to find where a copy-number change starts and stops.

blocks.html: A partial match scores half of its rung. A full match anywhere beats any partial match — even a full match down at rank 10.
one row contains EXACTLY the true pair. Partial match — a row contains one of the two true variants. Partial scores half.
the best F-score achievable by sweeping every epcr cut-off present in your file. Maxes at 1.0 only when your top row is exactly the true pair.
blocks.context: the field in the oracle's reply that carries the most information — the decode table is a lookup on it

blocks.html: trying each epcr value as a cut-off and keeping the best result. Consequence: rows below the best cut-off can never hurt you — extra low-confidence rows are FREE.

blocks.text:
true pair = {V1, V2}          your submitted file:

  rank  epcr   row contents
    1   0.95   V1 + V2      <- exactly the true pair
    2   0.80   V9 + V3
    3   0.40   V7

now cut the file at every epcr value that appears in it:

  cut at 0.95 -> you predicted {V1,V2}           P=2/2=1.00  R=1.00  F=1.00  <-- BEST
  cut at 0.80 -> you predicted {V1,V2,V9,V3}     P=2/4=0.50  R=1.00  F=0.67
  cut at 0.40 -> you predicted {V1,V2,V9,V3,V7}  P=2/5=0.40  R=1.00  F=0.57

  F-max = 1.00   (the best cut wins; the worse cuts are simply ignored)
blocks.legendHtml: each cut at line is one threshold in the sweep · P is precision, R is recall · the highest F wins and the rest are ignored.

blocks.html: So rows 2 and 3 could not lower your score. Secondary findings are genuinely free — add them.
if two rows share an epcr, order is decided by which came first. Avoid it: always use strictly different, descending epcr values.
submit 10 single variants to learn which of them is a true allele.
you know allele A; submit 10 pairs (A + each candidate) to find B.
the confirmed pair at rank 1, epcr 1.0. Maximum score.
